Review:
The L500 is a really nice and solidly built BMX at a great price. It looks very sharp with the chrome finish, green accents and minimal branding (which makes it look a lot more like a high end botique BMX compared to the L100 and lower models).

The main upgrade over the L100 model is a freecoaster hub which allows you to ride backwards/fakie without backpedaling, so that is really only applicable to advanced riders who are capable of bunny hopping into a 180 and riding backwards. The other upgrade over L100 is a half-link chain which allows more precise adjustment of the rear wheel position in the dropouts (but many riders prefer half-link chain because of how it looks more than caring about the adjustability factor)

So while the L500 model is great and I would recommend it to advanced riders who prefer a freecoaster hub.. the L100 model is definitely the best value and probably a better choice for most people.

Out of the box, it is mostly pre-assembled and really easy to put together even if you don't know much about working on bicycles, all you will need is a 5 mm and 6 mm hex wrench. That said, with this and any other new bike that's been shipped there are always going to be issues with the setup out of the box that will require more knowledge to fix, such as adjusting the brakes and truing the rims.. so if you don't know what you're doinig its best to take it to a local shop and pay them $50 or so to assemble and set it up.

My L500 weighs 25.2 lbs fully assembled (I replaced the included nylon pedals with metal pedals, so stock weight would have been slightly lower).

Review:
I had this bike for under five months, and logged about 330 miles on it; most of the miles were road miles around my town with varying elevations doing between 15-20mph, usually no less than 10 miles at a time. I would not recommend this bike to anyone who wants to use it for anything more than leisurely, slow rides around a neighborhood for the following reasons:

The first few rides, I had a pedal fall off (almost crashed), and the handlebars come loose; those may have been an issue with assembly and not tightening up enough, but it's not like I left everything so loose that those things should have happened. It got to the point where I always carried tools with me on my rides in case those things occurred again.

The chain skipped for almost the entirety of the time I used it over 4-5 months, and it eventually got to the point where downshifting to gears under maybe 13th gear caused the chain to grind horribly against the gears, sometimes popping the chain off.

It rusted at many different points (possibly from me sweating on it, but come on).

The gears were always difficult to get exactly in the correct position, brake adjustments were often required and they were always squeaky

The kicker of all these downsides occurred on my last ride, where downshifting at the end of the ride caused the chain to pop off the gear. It popped off while I had my full weight on a down-pedal and this cause the chain to get stuck around the derailleur and literally tear it off, bending the gears, snapping the housing, and rendering the bike completely unusable. Thankfully I purchased the coverage plan where I was fully reimbursed for the bike, but that is besides the point.

This is a definitely a you-get-what-you-pay for product, but I shudder to think what would happen to someone who took this on actual mountain bike trails. I fear someone could be seriously injured because of the poor quality. Buy at your own risk.

Review:
To preface this review, I should note that the company offers people who write a review on Amazon a free bell, which probably accounts for the large numbers of reviews this bike has. But the content of this review will not be influenced by the bell.

My history: I hadn't ridden a bike in about 15 years, but decided to buy one after renting bicycles for several months at a local park. I wanted a bicycle with good reviews that wasn't too expensive, and came upon this bike after weeks of research. I purchased it from the company's website when I saw they were having a sale for Memorial Day.

Assembly: maybe it's just because I'm so new to bikes, but assembly wasn't as easy as some of the reviews would lead you to believe. I ended up taking it to my local bike shop to have them assemble it, as I could not get the brake system to attach properly to the wheel. But I'm also not much of a mechanic, so maybe it's just me.

Appearance. It's beautiful! The paint scratches relatively easily (my cheap box-store watch scratched it when it accidentally bumped into it). It's reasonably heavy in a good way and feels sturdy. I think I'd have a hard time lifting it to put on a roof rack so if you're kinda weak like me, take that into consideration. It fits just fine in my trunk rack.

Function: it rides very well on paved surfaces. It almost feels like gliding on water - very smooth. I'm not a fan of the gear changing mechanism, which is a bit hard to change, especially when you're on the go. I mainly keep it in second gear as a result and rarely change it. I've only ridden it on paved roads around town so far and have yet to take it to a less polished trail. I've also ridden it in grass, which is a real pain, though I won't count that against the bike, as most bikes I've tried are bad in the grass.

I'll update this review when I've had more time with the bike, as I've only been riding less than a month. But so far I enjoy it! I'm interested to see if it holds up over the years and is worth the price tag. In my honest opinion, I wouldn't pay more than $399 for the bike. Keep an eye on their website for discount codes. I bought mine for $350 and feel that price is just right so far.

Review:
I have put almost 200 miles on the bike and have many good things to say, but a couple major complaints. First, the good:
PROS:
1. Great range! With practice and battery management skills, I'm sure you can get over 70 miles on a full charge. My first effort at 52 miles ended with still 2/5 bars showing (see photo). My latest trip was 43 miles with 3/5 bars left.
2. Great value. At $1,399, this is a lot of bike for the money.
3. Battery recharges on downhill rides! This is really fun, especially for me, an electric vehicle nerd. I love the way my EV recharges when coasting or braking. Now my bike does it, too. It also allows you to add to your workout. If you pedal while going downhill, it increases the charge rate while increasing your heart rate!
4. The battery has a USB outlet. No more dead cellphones!
5. Relatively light. Most large e-bikes can weigh 70 or 80 pounds. This one is under 50 with the battery removed. This is important for my bike carrier which is rated to 50 lbs.
6. Operates with throttle or peddle-assist. The throttle is really nice for starting up from a stoplight. It takes a couple cranks to get the assist going without it, so getting going by throttle really helps.
7. This bike can go fast on the flat. It cruises very comfortably with normal pedaling effort at 25 mph.
8. Tools needed for assembly were included... but no assembly instructions...which leads me to the....
CONS:
1. No paperwork included with the shipment. No assembly instructions, user manual, safety warnings, etc. Is that even legal? If you have never assembled a bike before, you'll probably need some help or at least find a good youtube video. There is an online user manual on the eahora website for the electric operation, but it is not particularly well written and contains some errors.
2. Some adjustments need to be made to make this comfortable. Not all the tools needed for those adjustments are included, so you need a good set of bike tools, especially allen wrenches. The gear shift thumb lever, for example, interferes with the grips, so I had to move it a couple inches to the left on the handlebar.
3. The motor has a mind of its own. It surges sporadically, sometimes when you don't want it. For example, I was turning sharply at a slow speed in a confined space when the motor kicked in, almost sending me crashing into a wall. THIS IS A SAFETY ISSUE THAT NEEDS TO BE CORRECTED. There are many adjustments that can be made on this bike, but the online instructions tell the user to contact customer support. I've done so. We'll see what they can do.
4. Because of the surging problem, this bike SHOULD NOT BE USED FOR MOUNTAIN TRAIL RIDING. MTB trails require careful control of speed, effort and direction. As this bike is sold to be used for trail riding, this is a major problem. If I had bought this bike for trail riding, I probably would have given it 1 star. I will use it primarily for pavement, gravel and dirt roads and flat trails.
5. The motor is not very powerful when going up hills. I am a pretty strong rider, so this is not a real issue with me, but it does take work getting up a hill. The power assist is certainly helpful, but underwhelming.

Would I buy this bike again, knowing what I know now? Probably not. But if customer service can correct the surge problem, I would change that to a yes.

August 1 UPDATE: Tech support was not very helpful. I sent them videos illustrating the problem but they said this is normal. So I decided to make some adjustments myself and was pleasantly surprised to find how easy the adjustments are. I was able to reduce but not eliminate the surging problem. I raised my rating to 4 stars, but if I could rate customer support separately, it would be 2 stars.

August 7 UPDATE: I discovered why there is so little help on the hills. For some reason, the pedal assist is limited to 6 amps, even at the highest setting. On the other hand, when you stop pedaling and use the throttle, the battery provides at least 15 amps and you can program it for more. I set mine so I now get 18 amps in throttle mode. However, as soon as you start pedaling, the assist level drops back to 6 amps max. I have alerted tech support to this so they can solve the problem. Hopefully they can help me reprogram the controller to either increase the level of amps in pedal assist mode, allow pedaling while using the throttle or send me a new controller that will allow me to tap into the power potential that is built into this bike.

I started biking after a 10 year hiatus over the summer. I was using a big heavy cruiser from a University bike-share program. I would go on bike trips with some of my friends who had hybrids and road bikes and quickly realized I needed a road bike that would allow me to keep up, but but didn't break the bank.

Assembly:

With my Topeak bike tool, assembly was no sweat. It took me 30 minutes to assemble the entire thing. The bike weighs exactly 29 pounds.

First Ride:

My first ride was a 10 mile jaunt around my town in New Jersey. Dawning my helmet and a tote bag with a pump, lock and tube, I was on my way. The ride was moderately smooth, I realized the front brake approached the point of uselessness. It took me 5 minutes to adjust this.

I am 6 feet and 220 pounds. After some research, I decided the 57cm variant was the best for me. The bike feels good and it is very responsive. Too make long rides a little more pleasant, I will shell out for a new seat.

The stock wheels are good. I don't see myself replacing them. The tires are good, but will be replaces with Cheng Shin tires as soon as I get the chance. I pump these up to 100 PSI with no problem. I am a fairly large person, so I will look into buying tubes that allow me to pump up till 125 PSI.

Handlebars:

These style handlebars are definitely hard to get used to. The tape seems solid and will definitely take normal wear and tear.

Shifters and Deraillers:

Out of the box, these work well. I have had only one loose chain. I will use Youtube to help me tweak these.

Overall, this is an excellent beginners bike. I recommend buying this.

Review:
I'm an inexperienced rider; 45 years old, 5'8", about 160-165 pounds. I say "inexperienced" although I used to ride all the time when I was a kid - rode proper road bikes in my teens and early 20s and all but gave it up since. I wanted to get back into riding after a doctor suggested regular exercise; I never liked running and my tolerance for treadmills, etc. is limited, but I remembered that I enjoyed riding when I was younger so I thought I'd get back into it. I'd had a Schwinn Caliente (24") and then I rode my brother's Schwinn LeTour II (or III, not sure) for a few years.
I tried a couple of Atlanta-area bike stores and was horrified to learn that the best I could do for a new bike was about $[...] for a last-year's model. Stores like Sports Authority had no road bikes at all. I was willing to pay in the $[...] range, but there simply wasn't anything.

I was worried about what I would get for the price, but I told myself that really, all I was looking for was a more or less direct replacement for the LeTour; I'm not trying to be Lance.

By way of clarification, this appears to be a Chinese-made Kent bicycle, re-badged as a "GMC Denali." I don't think that this branding is counterfeit; I think this bicycle was produced as part of a GM SUV promotion (i.e., buy an SUV; get a bike free) and they had a LOT of bikes left over. As some have noted, it is a weird agglomeration of parts with its twist shifters and mountain-bike gearing. It's attractive; the photo does not do the electric deep blue pearl finish justice. In sunlight, it's amazing.

So far I've ridden it up to thirteen miles in traffic on moderately hilly roads and up to sixteen miles on a flat coastal road with a proper bike lane. I'm not very in-shape so sometimes I have to drop it into 1/1 and creep to go uphill.

Shifters. Once the limits were set, the chain hasn't been dropping off the edges. To take the rear gear reliably from, say, 3 to 4, you might have to twist the thing 3-5-4 to really get it set properly. I have not had any tooth jumping. On flat road, I'm finding myself going between 3/6 and 3/7; I don't know if this means I need a taller sprocket somewhere or not.

Several people talked about punctured tubes almost as soon as they started riding the bike. The first time that happened to me, I think I pinched it coming into the driveway with the pressure at about 90PSI (it needs to be 100 the max at my weight and when I set off I take it to 105, assuming that it will be down to 100 at the end of my ride). However, I lost a tube again for no good reason and I investigated. It turns out that there was little or no cleanup after the spoke nut holes were drilled out and several of the holes had sharp crescent-shaped metal shards attached to them. I went around both wheels with a rattail file and got rid of all that and I replaced the thin rubber liners with heavier-duty ones. The wheels on my bike were reasonably straight and true.

I started wondering about what I perceived to be excessive rolling drag so I pulled off the wheels to turn the shafts by hand and they felt pretty crunchy and stiff on both ends; I stayed off the bike subsequently and had them rebuilt at a bike shop but I'm not sure how much better they are - the drag seems better at least. I would suggest having these bearings checked and repacked not long after you get the bike. They are of an old-school sort and I learned that not all bike shops can even really work on them.
The tires have held up pretty well for having been pinched and having been removed and put on a few times; I have a pair of Michelin replacements but I expect I'll keep the OEMs on until they pop or wear out. They are 700x28c and I have yet to see tires that size in a bike shop or anywhere else; you'd better mail-order one or two and keep them as a spare because you may not be able to find one local to you.

I replaced the seat with a Bontrager that has the center groove and opening.

The brakes could be a lot better; the caliper arms bend appreciably during use. When I had the wheel bearings overhauled, I tried to have the shop replace the calipers outright but they did not have any that would fit. I'm finding the angle of the brake levers awkward. This is one area where you might consider making some changes as soon as you get the bike. You might consider taping up the rubber brake lever housing boots as soon as you get the bike because I've already torn up one and there's no point in fixing them. You don't strictly need them as they're really only there for a little padding; I wear padded Bell gloves anyway, so I'm fine in that regard.

It made me nervous going really fast downhill initially; it's harder than I remember it being back in the day to hold the bike in line going around a turn at speed; I feel like it's a geometry and weight-distribution problem and not necessarily a flaw of the bicycle, but it will be interesting to see if it's any different with new tires. With the tires pumped up to 100PSI going really fast can make your eyeballs vibrate too much to see clearly if the road is rough (raising butt up off the seat even just a little sorts that right out).

So to sum up, if you buy this bike and really want to ride it 1) replace the seat, although the original isn't horrible 2) make sure everything's adjusted 3) put some time, money, and attention into the brakes 4) clean up the wheel machining and upgrade the liners *immediately* 5) have at least one spare tube and tire on hand.

Review:
We bought two of these bikes--one for my 2.5 year old and one for my 1.5 year old. Here's what we've found:

-The younger one is short so we sawed off a bit of the seat post in order to get the seat lower and it allllmost fits her.

-it's hard for the kids to figure out which way the handle bars go. We attached a basket to the front to help a bit and that works well. Still, the handle bars turn all the way around and look almost the same whether they're facing the correct way or wrong way.

-the tires ripped open on one of them. I called the manufacturer and they shipped two new tires without asking any questions. No hassle. It was great. I don't know why the tires ripped open because I'd filled them properly and it doesn't get very cold or hot where we live.

-having air in the tires makes for a great and smooth ride for the kids. It's also quiet.

-we love having the adjustable seat. The handlebars don't adjust, but we haven't needed that. By the time we would need that, the kids will be on peddle bikes.

-there is a foot platform that my younger daughter can rest her feet on while we push her. Since she can't reach the ground while sitting on the seat, the platform is nice to help her understand the concept of riding a bike.

-the foot platform gets very scratched every time the bike falls. We are mountain bikers so we don't mind scratched bikes.

All in all, we are very happy with this bike!

Review:
I got my bike 2nd hand from my boss who never rode it. Literally rode it three times and it gathered dust in his garage! So, after my car broke down he sold me this bike for $60, originally paying around $200 for it I believe.

I get a lot of compliments on the paint job for this bike, a real nice shiny blue and silver. It's a road bike frame and handlebars with a mountain bike gearing system which labels this a "hybrid." it's 3 in the front and 7 in the back - not a typical setup for a real road bike, which would have 2 gears in the front and 8-10 gears in the back. I NEVER use 1st in the front, and heck, I don't even believe my bike can switch into that gear.

I personally did not like the action of the cheap end Shimano Touring rear derailleur - I upgraded to a Shimano Alivio on the rear derailleur and it shifts MUCH better, so much better, and it was only a $32 part at my local bike shop.

I can hit 28mph with some serious pedalling and maintain the distance comfortably on the bike. I would suggest getting
quick-change rim setups on the bike, $50/ea at my bike shop. Totally makes the difference if you run a flat or blow a tire while riding. Ever walked home before from a distance ride? Pfft... sucks!

If you are looking for a nicely priced bike, I would say that this will meet your needs. Better to spend the $$$ on this than a $400-$600 GIANT if you are just testing the waters on cycling for fitness or for fun.

BY THE WAY, this bike is made by KENT BICYCLES out of NJ. Took me forever to figure that out because I needed some replacement parts. Just FYI!

Review:
I have ridden bikes for years, but this bike (Tommaso Monza) is my first road bike. Before settling on this bike, I tried to buy a Schwinn bike, believing that’s a more established brand. After Schwinn seller failed to deliver the product twice, I started looking for alternatives. I was attracted by the good customer rating and high road bike sales rank of Tommaso bikes on Amazon. So I made the purchase. One month later, here are my initial impressions of this bike. 1) The bike represents good value for entry level road bike. I am looking for a lighter bike with good gears, so I can reach better speed than using my current mountain bike or other leisure bike. With a weight of little over 20 pounds this bike is much lighter than my current bikes, the Shimano gear also works well. Other brands (like Schwinn) selling at higher prices with lower quality gears. I immediately got a 15% boost in speed from my first serious ride on this new bike. I think more improvements will come. 2) The manufacturer delivered product on time and in good condition. With all the supply chain issues caused by the pandemic, this is not a given. 3) I was planning to let a bike shop put bike together for me, but after watching an instruction video on the company’s web site I feel it’s easy enough to assemble the bike myself. The bike came in ready for assembling, just need to put the handle bar and front wheel in and tighten the screws with Allen keys (not included with the bike). I did need to watch more YouTube videos to learn how to adjust the brakes, but I feel that’s good learning experience for me to have a little bit more knowledge about bikes in general. 4) One reason I chose this bike is it’s size. At 5’7” I normally fall between size Small and Medium. That leaves the question of which size I should choose open. With Tommaso I happen to solidly fit into size Small according to the company’s sizing chart. I verified the detailed geometric information (like the length of the top tube, seat tube, stand-over height etc.) and compared them with other brands. I felt confidently enough that the bike size will fit me well to make the online purchase without actually trying the bike. So far I feel the new bike size fits me well. I’ve had this bike for about 6 months now. For my needs it’s perfect and has held up well. I’ve been around town with it, on longer trips on the road, in the mountains on pretty rugged trails, and for a 15 mile beach ride (on the wet sand). Although it’s on the heavy side (50 lbs.) you can still conserve your battery and ride it with no power on a flat road or put it in the first power level and get a small extra boost that makes it ride like a lighter bike. At the highest power setting I can easily get it up to 24 mph without pedaling very hard. It also has a throttle for no pedaling power so if you’re tired you can cruise without pedaling and enjoy the scenery.

For the price you get a lot including hydraulic disc brakes, shimano gears, tubeless tires, 3 power modes . Don’t expect it to be a high end mountain bike (which could easily cost 2 to 3 times as much). The components are descent (the quality of the hydraulic brakes is just ok, they work fine but mine make a bit of a rubbing sound). If you don’t want to spend a lot, aren’t looking for a high end electric mountain bike, and want versatility with a long power range than I would recommend this bike.

Review:
My 26-inch 3-speed Urban Lady ("Vanilla" color, which is actually more of a creamy-bright yellow, like eggnog!) is a rock solid bike, lovely to look at, and a joy to ride. From a childhood spent on "sting ray" style bikes (relatively low & upright seating position) with "banana" seats, as an adult I've never been able to feel comfortable or confident on bikes that require that you sit high and lean forward. So recently I figured, heck, I'm in my mid-fifties... why shouldn't I be able to ENJOY riding a bike, who cares what "everybody else" is riding?? I get lots of smiles & compliments every time I take my Urban Lady for a spin-- we're an unusual sight in my urban environment!
Note: the bike is quite heavy, and its kickstand is a bit anemic; I replaced the kickstand with a double-legged one that swings handily out of the way, to the side just like the stock kickstand. Also note, the color of the fenders is NOT a particularly good match to the color on the bikes; they don't "clash," but you can easily tell they come from different dye lots. Finally, while the seat may be comfortable to some, I did not find it so; I replaced it with a cushier one, and then also added a gel bike seat pad on top of that... heaven! :-)

Now for the unpleasant parts of my buying experience:
I am completely bewildered by the glowing customer service reviews /comments that BeachBikes has for the various bikes they sell in Amazon. I got a better price by buying directly from the BeachBikes website, so I dealt directly with them. Here's my story:
I initially purchased a 26" bike, then thought I might be more comfortable on a smaller one, so ordered a 24" to try out (they have a good return policy). In the end I decided to keep the larger bike.
1) the BB website did not have 26" fenders visible for order with my first bike, so I had to call to order it. Never got email confirmation/tracking # of the fender order, so several days later I had to email them and ask for it. It took a couple of days for them to get back to me.
2) The link to a video with assembly instructions was sent with their delayed reply; the model did not exactly match the bike I had purchased, and some of the videography and instructions were too vague-- one of the results of this was that if it were not for my husband noticing, I would have been trying to ride around with my front wheel fork facing in the wrong direction.
3) They claim that every customer gets assigned their own "personal mechanic" to field questions during assembly; my mechanic must have been fired or was out on vacation, because I never got any help. Halfway through assembly i ran into a problem so I called during their business hours. I was sent to their voicemail, and NEVER received a return call in spite of having left a detailed message. Thank goodness I have a few basic mechanical skills, so I figured out what I needed to do. I know they're a brick&mortar with live customers to serve, but calling customers back, at least within 48 hours, should not be too much to ask. I've called them three additional times during their hours, at different times of day, and have NEVER had a human answer the phone. Email replies from them are also inappropriately delayed-- several days, and sometimes they need an extra email to remind them that you emailed them the first time!
4) Once I had tried out both the 26" and 24" bikes, I made my decision about which one to keep. I DID get good packing instructions from customer service, and (with no small effort) was able to get the bike back into its box, and the fenders back into theirs. Shipped it all FedEx Ground using labels BeachBikes provided, with notes inside the box stating my name & order #. I have FedEx confirmation that BeachBikes received & signed for my packages two weeks ago... but they have still NOT contacted me confirming my return, NOR have they initiated a credit to my credit card.

Based on the reviews on Amazon mentioning BeachBikes' customer service, it may well be that they are choosing to focus their service efforts on Amazon customers; my experience says that if you deal with them directly, you are definitely NOT a priority or a valued customer,
The bike itself deserves 4 stars (one star off for the weak kickstand and for one particularly nasty quirk in its assembly requirements); since this is a "product" review and not a "seller" review, I don't want to penalize the bike for BeachBikes' behavior, so I have resisted the impulse to rate it 2 or 3 stars because of them.

Review:
This review will focus on assembly and overall impressions only. This is a Christmas gift and it is only late September so I won't know about the bike's durability and functionality for another three months or more. What can I say, my wife likes to get her shopping done early! Also, if you are looking for a bike to pass on to future generations of young riders, you might want to look at something a little more expensive than this one. But at this price point there is nothing to lead me to reject this out of hand as a trainer for one or more siblings.

Tools are included for assembly, but they are not really the best. But I used the included whale shaped multi tool to tighten all nuts as I wanted to ensure that someone receiving this would be able to complete the task. Unfortunately, the included hex head wrench proved to be useless as it did not fit any of the handlebar assembly bolts. For those with access to proper tools I recommend you have a 14mm open end wrench and a 6mm hex head hex. In addition, the reflectors need a #2 Philips screw driver which was not included.

Instructions for assembly are in a little booklet and are rudimentary, but if you've seen a bicycle before you should be able to follow them without much trouble, even if you are mechanically challenged.

Assembly consists of mounting the front wheel, the training wheels, pedals to crank, seat, and handlebars. Reflectors are optional but recommended so make sure you slip them on to the seat post and handle bar stem prior to mounting those items.

The training wheels just require you to remove the rear axle nuts and round washers, slip one on each side and replace the round washer and nut on each side and tighten. It is nice that these are included, but I hope my grandson learns to ride without them in about a month because I can't believe the inexpensive plastic outrigger wheels will last much longer than that.

Front wheel is similar in nature, remove the two nuts and locking "clips", drop the axle into the fork slots replace the clip washers and nuts and retighten. Make sure the locking clips engage in the fork holes to ensure the axle will not work out of the front fork slots.

The handle bar requires you to loosen the tightening mechanism slightly so that you can slide it into the steering head tube. Remember to slide the clear front reflector onto the shaft first and slightly tighten. Align the bar with the front wheel and using the 6mm hex head, tighten it securely.

The seat simply requires you to slip on the rear red reflector, slide the down tube into the frame and then rotate the locking lever until snug and tighten the assembly by closing the "clasp"

The pedals come with a clearly marked R and L demarcation. As I remember the L screws in counter clockwise. Securely tighten nuts with either the whale wrench or your own 14mm open wrench.

Adjust seat height and training wheel height to accommodate rider's needs.

I don't know who to blame for these issues, was it manufacturing? was it shipping? was it distribution? I don't know. What I know is the state of what I got, and here it what I got:

The front tire was irreparably warped. Minor wobbles can be fixed simply by tightening or loosening the spokes. Which was required for both front and back wheels upon arrival, but this is expected. What was not expected is that the front wheel was warped so extremely that, although you can still ride the bike, you can see it wobble as you are riding it.

All of the stickers were starting to peel or was damaged; probably due to poor handeling and parts hitting it as it was being shipped, for all the parts (wheel, handlebar, main body/rearwheel, pedals where not neatly stowed away in some snuggly fitting foam, or cardboard, but it looked like they just tossed it all into the box and said "it's no longer our problem what happens to it." Some parts of the paint were chipped. The pedal was broken, which is amazing because it looks like a metal alloy, aluminum perhaps, and it is snapped in half.

Also the front fork was about 1 inch narrower than the wheel so it was impossible to get the wheel in. I had to get the crank from my car that is used to lift the car when you change your tire to open it up a bit so that the frame will deform a bit. This step was by far the most stressful (among truing the wheel, adjusting the break pads, adjusting the break wires).

So far there doesn't seem to be any issue with the chain, crank, cogs, breaks etc. rides fine; it's just a crappy quality.

I took off all of the stickers and the neon green handlebar grips so that the body is completely black and the handlebar is completely grey. It is a pretty good looking bike, I must say. Also a part of the handlebar was missing paint. Not that it was chipped off, but that it simply lacked spraypaint.

also, in case this is your first purchase of a BMX bike, you should know one thing: you can't really do any tricks with this. The bike weighs about 3 times as much as my road bike, that is, this BMX bike weighs like 35 pound. Try spinning this thing around. Good luck. The ones where you can actually do tricks are the ones that cost like +$300. Also the fact that this has 24 inch wheels means it's practically as big as a small mountain bike so don't plan on being a bad ass with this. It is a cruiser substitute. It moves, and it breaks.

I would not buy this as a gift to anyone for it just LOOK crappy (irrespective of the quality).

I don't care about the looks and I plan on tossing this away after a year or so., leaving it out in the sun and rain until than, only to be used to travel about 1 mile/day to go to my coffee shop. If you want a bike to take care of and grow old with, get something that is worth protecting.

The tires are a bit flimsy, and they came barely inflated. If you simply add air, you might blow the bead off the rim if you aren't careful. You need to massage them until the bead seats evenly. The grandkids had three flats in the first month from tiny seed pods, so I installed liners and Slime tubes. The fenders are flimsy, perhaps a hazard because the rear fenders have come loose.
Even without power, I like the feel of the bicycles. The disc brakes work great. (I hope pads will be available). The shifting is quite nice. The front suspension also feels nice, but might be too soft for aggressive riders, and the seals weep a little. Power feels fairly good, speed isn't, but local laws require 20mph cut-out in order to be categorized for unlicensed riders under 16 years old.
One of the batteries had a minor defect. The receptacle wasn't tightened down, and the dust plug fell off it's mount the first day that bicycle was used. I removed the lower cover from the battery pack, melted the adhesive with a soldering iron, loosened the nut far enough to reinstall the dust plug, tightened the nut, and reflowed the thermal adhesive. It's been fine so far.
The kickstand design is very nice, the toe-to-front-wheel clearance is good. These bicycles look sharp. I would buy them again, and might even buy a third one. The price is very appealing.

Review:
This review is for the Huffy Hardtail Mountain Trail Bike - 26 inch wheels/20 inch frame, Gloss Nickel.

I was not much of a biker and have not rode a bike in ten years. When looking for a "bike", was not sure what to get or what to look for when purchasing online (i.e. can't try it out before purchasing). I picked this model mainly because of the low cost ($275.00) and good reviews. Next, I was not even sure how to pick the frame size or wheel size. After some internet reading, the 20-inch frame size was the best option for my 5'10 height and chose the 26-inch wheel size (seemed proportional to the 20-inch frame). My main objective was "joy" riding and not really doing any biking on mountains or off-road biking.

The bike came in new - very little assembly. Only had to install the front tire and the handle bar assembly. The packaging include a multi-purpose tool (wrench) and hex wrenches to assembly the bike.

Once the bike was assembled, I had two issues:
1. The rubber brake pads were slightly rubbing against the rim. I had to play around with it a bit to adjust the brakes. Was able to adjust them where they were perfect.

2. Now, the hard part. The front derailleur was not working correctly. I could not shift into some of the gears and could also hear slight clicking/tapping when peddling. Very long story short, I had to watch many videos on YouTube on how to adjust the derailleur (i.e. low/high limits, cable tension..etc). Also, without a bike stand to hold up the bike, this becomes a tedious effort. For those of you who have had to do this, you know the pain. So, after many many hours of adjusting the limits and cable tension, got it to where it is 99% better when using the gear shifters (from and back).

The bike size fits me perfect. No issues with comfort in riding. I can easily adjust the seat height and handle bars for a better fit.

Overall, this is a decent mountain bike for what I need it for. Not looking for anything special. I do enjoy riding it and happy with the purchase. If you are looking for a bike for cruising or joy riding, then a mountain bike is not for you. (mainly because of the treads on the wheels).

Couple items to know about:

1. Change out the bike seat ASAP. Too hard and causes pain/rash within 15min of riding.

2. If you remove the front derailleur tension cable, make sure you put it back on the correct way or else the gear lever will not work. It will feel tight and you will not be able to shift any gear. I learned this the hard way after I spent about three hours trying to figure out why I could not shift the gear lever. Finally, I realized my very simple mistake. When you wrap the tension cable around the locking nut, you need to loop it in a clockwise motion, not counter clockwise. - lesson learned. (see attached picture).

Review:
This ebike exceeded my expectations. The battery lasts around two hours depending on how much the throttle is used. The battery lasts longer using the pedal assist only. It was fairly easy to put together. This ebike has changed the way I view going for a bike ride. It is so much easier to justify biking somewhere instead of driving. I'll take it on small trips to the grocery store or on miles long trips to the other side of town.

I get outside more and enjoy the fresh air without overworking myself. Don't get me wrong, you definitely still have to pedal unless you only use the throttle. However, the resistance is significantly less compared to pedaling a non motor bike. Going uphill is when some real resistance can be felt, but the battery takes you right up the hill without you breaking a sweat.

The battery takes a few hours to charge. It has some weight to it and is kind of large. The bike itself weighs roughly 40lbs which makes it difficult to maneuver. You need to store it indoors because the rain is an ebikes enemy. Getting it up the three steps into to the house is a chore. Other than those couple cons, this bike is a real game changer, I have gone on more adventures than I could have imagined in a the couple months of having it. I definitely will be ordering a more comfortable seat and possibly a rack for the back tire.
I am very pleased with how easy this bike is to use. The buttons are easy to read and easy to use quickly. Sometimes you have to switch from the pedal assist to throttle only to no motor in a short amount of time, i.e. going around a sharp turn in town. The buttons on other bikes I have seen have been in odd positioning, but not on this bike. There is also a gauge for the battery life left. This is helpful if the ride is longer, so you know when the halfway point is and turn around.
Great purchase overall.

After several months with this bike, I could scarcely be happier. Sure, I'd love it to be a bit lighter, but for the price, I am THRILLED.

I use it mostly for that last mile commute in NYC- getting the mile from the subway to home or destination. And it's perfect- i dont even need to fold it for the subway, I can carry it through a turnstyle. I can't speak to mileage, since ive never used it for a long commute, or tried to go till the battery was empty. The pedal assist is intuitive and great. I will say, trying to pedal this without any power at all is not fun- the wheels are small and there's no gears, so it's rough going. Do not plan to get stuck without power. And it takes 3-4 hrs to refill fully from our home outlet, and thats not from empty- usually about 3-4 bars. I dont know how long it would take from empty.

It folds up compactly so if space is an issue, this wont take up much. In a NYC apt, that means alot.

My biggest complaint was the seat- it's narrow, not well padded and without any gap in the middle as most modern seats have to take pressure off your perineal nerve. It started to get pretty painful- so I bought a new seat on Amazon for $20! That's been great. So, if they would just include a good seat, this bike would be perfect.

Review:
My favorite things about this bike, in order:
1. You can't put the seat all the way down without sitting it in the baby seat. The best part here is that you can either: A. Raise the seat two inches higher so a baby will fit, and then your daughter will fall on their face when they try to climb in the too-high seat, or: B. Lower the seat down so your kid can sit in the seat, and then they will whine all day because they can't get their baby in the seat. (Bonus: The baby seat is made of flimsy plastic attached by metal screws, so it should be broken off after just a couple uses (bonus bonus: probably leaving sharp pieces of plastic behind!)!)
2. There's a great part on the instructions where it says, "If you bought the other components, such as the mudguards, basket, kick stand, please read the corresponding instructions to install them." I was disappointed because I thought for sure they were going to leave these things off the instructions. Luckily though, after searching through every paragraph I realized that they wouldn't disappoint...the instructions they told you to check don't exist! So now I got to spend 20 minutes trying to figure out how to attach the basket (there's secret zip tie type things that are the same color as the basket zip tied to the bottom of the basket, hiding in plain sight!). To install the reflector I got to open up Amazon so I could look at the photos (which helped me remember to leave this review.) I saw that to install the reflector the handlebars had to be raised up some (can't be at the lowest setting otherwise my tiny kid might have too easy of a time with it!) So now that I was done assembling the bike, I got to disassemble it and raise the handlebars and re-straighten everything just to fit the reflector on.
3. The "bell". Those quotation marks are there on purpose. Look for any metal object near you, and strike it was another metal object. That's a "bell", as far as the bike manufacturer here is concerned. That's all it is - it's not a real "bwing bwing" classic bike bell...it's a bell-looking piece of metal with another piece of metal next to it, which you pull down on some rubber attached to a spring to hopefully have it clack against the "bell" and make a tiny "dink". Amazing. No more worrying about your bicycle bells annoying (or warning) passers-by with this one. Luckily for me the bell broke off when I tried to assemble it and now can never be installed. If you want the bell tight enough so it doesn't spin when you push it, know that you'll likely rip through the plastic connecting pieces with minimal torque. Have fun.

They sell bikes for half the price at Walmart...they'll probably be terrible bikes, but hey, this is a terrible bike too, so you win either way. Save your money, go to Walmart. While you're there at least you can pick up a real bell.

Review:
Review for HiBoy P7:
I am very happy with this eBike overall and I would highly recommend it. It came well packaged in a very strong box so there were no issues with damage in shipment. Assembly was easy and the only adjustment I had to make other than seat height was on the front brake because of some rubbing. The bike is well made with nice welds and a high quality finish. The battery is integral to the frame which gives the bike a very nice look like eBikes that are much more expensive.
My first test ride was about 15 miles on level and hilly paved roads. What I found was that I could not go faster than 18.1 MPH in gear 9 on level roads in P5, even if I stood up and pedaled as fast as I could. It was the weekend, so I waited until Monday to contact HiBoy support via phone. After calling and getting a recording, I got a call back as promised in the recording and the person nicely told me that he couldn’t help me directly with technical issues with the bike- his only function was to direct me to contact support via email. That was not very efficient, but I have to say, once I contacted HiBoy support via email, they were very responsive.
I was contacted back via email overnight by Kaya from the support team. Since the emails are coming from China, I typically received them between 9pm and 5am EST. Kaya said that the controller was limiting the speed to 18 MPH, (which is 28 Km/ hr), and he would send me a new one to remove the speed limit. He did not explain why the first controller was programmed to limit the speed to 18 MPH when the Amazon listing stated in multiple places that the top speed would be 28 MPH. Maybe there was confusion over kilometers vs miles per hour?
I received the new controller in about 10 days. Kaya had kindly made and sent an instructional video so it was easy to install the new controller in about 15 minutes.
I took the same test ride route and the performance was dramatically different. Before, it felt like I was riding an Exercycle when I reached 18 MPH, now I was able to reach 21.5 MPH in P5 when pedaling normally on level road and 23.5 MPH when pedaling hard. The battery level also remained higher than with the previous controller. This is OK for my purposes, but I contacted Kaya because the Amazon listing stated I should be able to reach 28 MPH.
As always, Kaya replied promptly overnight and instructed me to perform a test which involved operating the bike in throttle only mode and then moving the pedals with the rear wheel in the air in P5. I reported back that I was able to reach 23.4 MPH with throttle only and 29 to 30 MPH while moving the pedals. Although Kaya replied back that the engineers said that was within specifications, I believe their description on Amazon should be changed to reflect “real world” speed on level road for person of average weight, (165 lbs)- that is, 23 MPH. The only way to reach 28 MPH would be on a downhill stretch, so I think it is a little disingenuous to state otherwise and it only serves to give a customer unreasonable expectations. That being said, I am perfectly happy with the performance of this bike now that I know what I should expect and I am very happy I bought it. At $999. current price, it is an outstanding value compared to any other eBikes with batteries integral to the frame that I saw listed on Amazon.
The improvements I would like to see HiBoy make are:
1) Change the website description and specifications to more accurately reflect the top speed of 23 MPH that a user could reasonably expect. The engineers know full well that if the top speed is 29 or 30 MPH when testing with no load, that when adding 225 lbs, (the weight of bike and average rider combined), it would be virtually impossible to reach a speed of 28 MPH without the help of gravity, as in, downhill. I was only able to reach 28 MPH when pedaling downhill, (incidentally, if coasting downhill, the speed will be limited and gradually reduce to 23 MPH depending on the grade). The top speed should be listed as 23 MPH, not 28 MPH.
2) Increase front sprocket size slightly for slower pedaling at top speed.
3) Provide ergonomic hand grips that are more comfortable on wrists. It is difficult to find aftermarket replacement grips because the right side grip is a half twist throttle grip.
4) Add rear LED taillight for safety with switch, same as included headlight which is excellent. Headlight and taillight could be operated by same switch since it is powered by bike’s own battery.
5) Provide larger mode/ speed display with the ability to make some adjustments to the controller with settings via the mode/ speed display. Display is OK to read but power and setting buttons are small and close together, so it is hard to change settings while riding, particularly when wearing gloves.

All in all, I would not hesitate to recommend this eBike, even without the above improvements. If the website description was changed to reflect a more accurate real world top speed, I would rate it 5 stars, but as it is, my rating is 4 stars. If the description and specs are changed on Amazon and on the HiBoy website, I will happily change my rating to 5 stars.

Review:
We bought two of these bikes for my husband and I to ride around the neighborhood or take while we're camping. The shipment was excellent as they arrived earlier than expected (shipment was from NJ or somewhere in the NE) and the boxes were intact with no damage. Husband assembled both bikes and said, for the most part, the instructions were pretty clear and he was able to figure out the confusing parts.

The bike is sturdy and heavy, around 60 lbs. It's foldable and folds at the frame, but the handle and pedals don't fold and the bike is still bulky and heavy when trying to insert the folded bike into the cargo area of a hatchback car. We ended up having a hitch installed on one of our cars and purchasing a sturdy bike rack (from Amazon) that would carry at least 120 lbs. in order to transport these bikes whenever we wanted to take them to the greenways in our city.

The battery is large and heavy, but there is a bag that carries it at the handlebar so it's easily removable to bring the battery into the house to charge it. There are 2 cords leading out of the battery, one to charge it and another to connect it to the bike. You have to thread the connection cord through the small hole at the bottom of the bag in order to connect it to the bike wiring, and that is a bit of a headache to work it through the hole.

The controller to activate the pedal assist works pretty well while cycling. It activates within 2 seconds of holding down the on/off switch and you can feel it kick in to propel you forward. I usually turn it off when I am going through tight spaces like a small, narrow bridge or lane to stay in control of the bike, but definitely use the pedal assist feature on incline and hills. We have hilly terrain in our subdivision and some streets require me to use the medium setting to get to the top of the hill, and it does it quite easily. The low setting is usually enough for me to get around. I haven't needed to use the high setting because so far the med setting gets me up the steeper streets. There is a throttle on the right side of the handlebar that allows you to use the pedal assist feature continuously without pedaling but I haven't needed to use it often. I definitely love the pedal assist feature to get up those hilly streets!

We had to switch the seats to wider seats because the one that comes with the bike is very narrow and uncomfortable. We also got sturdier and louder bells as the one that came with the bike is lousy and has a puny sound. We added bottle holders easily to the bike frame since there were 2 screws for that purpose already on the frame. I do wish they would have included mirrors to help when we're maneuvering and turning on the street. That's something else we'll have to buy. Also, there is no speedometer but I found an app for my phone to help monitor my speed and distance.

The fenders are kind of flimsy but they work. At my height of 5'3", the height of the bike is okay and I can easily stand on the balls of my feet when the bike is stopped, but I end up hitting and kicking the back fender regularly when getting on the bike, and I have to straighten it up.

We're really happy with these bikes and so far haven't had any major issues (knock on wood.) We especially love the lower cost for this electric bike and that it looks good, works very well, and has a year warranty.

Review:
Some months ago, I bought the 26" 3-speed "Around the Block" cruiser and decided recently to buy this 24" single-speed "Around the Block" cruiser for our 10-year-old daughter. The bike arrived promptly in a week and assembly took about an hour. Since there are no hand brakes to deal with, you basically only need to assemble the front tire, the handlebar, the seat/saddle, the pedals, and the rear rack. Having a set of wrenches (especially in sizes 9/16 and metric 15) would greatly help with tightening properly all the bolts. It is also a good idea to buy a small WD-40 spray and coat well the coils under the seat - those tend to creek after a while unless oiled properly.

The only issue I had with the bike was the valve of one of the tires - it was difficult (for some reason) to make it work with my bike pump, but I was able after several attempts to inflate properly the tire to about 45-50 PSI.

Other observations: the teal color is nice and the bike itself behaves very well on the road - no loose bearings, clonking pedals, or squeaking saddle coils. The rear coaster break is very responsive and easy to use. I also added a handlebar mirror (this model fits great: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B06XWRMZZF) as a safety precaution. The only downside is the seat/saddle - it is hard, and I mean HARD. Certainly not comfortable.

My impressions of the "Around the Block" cruisers are generally positive - they are not without issues, but are a step above what one could find in stores like Target, Walmart, or Meijer.

Review:
After purchasing this bike I can confidently say this is the best value, 16 inch, premium bicycle available on the market. I researched bicycles for my four and a half year old extensively and I try to submit a review for any product that I believe is truly a quality product. That said, when I stumble across an excellent product, I try to communicate such so as to ensure that the value is recognized and so that more expansive products will hopefully follow suit and come to market from that company as a result of the recognition. To this point, after extensive research, this bike came into play because of having hand brakes (no coaster brake), light weight, belt drive, high quality components, great geometry and overall value considering the aforementioned.

Before getting into details about the bike, let me me first say that I'm submitting this review about six hours after receiving the bicycle earlier today. Not only is the bike solidly built and phenomenal looking in person but my son who had been riding a balance bicycle rode this bicycle without my help on the first day. I received this bicycle from Amazon two days earlier than initially expected on April 14, 2020 at about 10:00AM Eastern time and my son was riding on his own just after 12:00 in the afternoon. To say that it blew me away is an understatement!!! Needless to say, he doesn't want to stop riding and I attribute that a great deal to the excellent geometry, solid components, lightweight frame (and killer looks) of this bicycle.

First, this bike has adjustable, hand brakes as opposed to coaster brakes. Many of the less expensive department store bicycles have a coaster and in fact coaster brakes are what many of us learned to ride with. However, with product research and product evolutions, have come better ways to do things. One example of this is the advent of balance bikes (as an alternative to training wheels) as a precursor to riding a bicycle. As mentioned, seeing was believing today because my son got on this bicycle and rode within fifteen to twenty minutes of pushing himself along (as he did with his balance bike). I am planning to post a video. As such, hand brakes for children, as opposed to coaster brakes, have become a most desirable way of braking due to their strong braking power on both front and rear wheel whereas coaster brakes only brake on the rear wheel. Also, the absence of the coaster brake on the crankset, results in children not stopping suddenly if they should pedal backward accidentally (which children often tend to do when learning to ride a bicycle without training wheels – their reflexes cause them to pedal backward when they are trying to ride and balance the bike and this causes them to stop and fall off the bike). Lastly, with coaster brakes, you cannot freely move the pedals backward so it’s harder for a child to get the pedals in the 2 o’clock and 8 o’clock position when they are trying to start off riding and want one of the pedals in the up position. In short, hand brakes make it easier for them to rotate the pedals and step and go. As mentioned initially, it’s important to note that some hand brakes are not adjustable but adjustable hand brakes are all the more imperative for a child’s hand because it allows you to dial in the right reach to ensure that your child’s hand can grasp the brake lever according to their hand size – super important. The Belsize has adjustable hand brakes which is a premium feature and absolutely necessary.

Secondly, this bike is about 13 pounds. Weight is extremely important for younger riders particularly when training wheels come off. Most department store bikes are in the 21-25 pound range which essentially means that if you have a little one who is say, 40 pounds, for example, they would be trying to hold up half their weight, or more, when trying to ride a typical 16 inch department store bicycle of 21 plus pounds. To put it differently, for adults that ride bikes, it’s like a 180 pound adult holding up a 90 pound bike but in fact, even worse for a child because a young child’s strength isn’t proportional to their weight at such a young age. Therefore, 20 plus pounds is heavy particularly when they’re trying to learn something like getting on and off a bicycle. A heavy bike simply results in the experience being less fun and like anything else, they won’t use the bicycle as often due to getting tired and frustrated. That said, the Belsize 16 is lighter than most of the premium name bicycles that are out there and in fact, I only found ONE other comparable, premium bicycle out there that was as light or lighter and that well known kid’s bike manufacturer (that begins with a “W”) weighs in at just under 12 pounds and retails for just under $400 but DOES NOT have a belt drive. (As an aside, I like the geometry on the Belsize bicycle much better than the previously mentioned bike.) That alone makes the Belsize 16 a superior value.

Thirdly, as mentioned above, this bicycle has a belt drive which is a more costly and longer lasting drive system than the conventional chain drives that bikes have been made with for years. Belt drives are a new innovation and they’ve gained in popularity in kids bikes and adult bikes, alike. The belt drive is known for it’s ease of maintenance and clean attributes because it doesn’t need to be oiled, cleaned or adjusted like a bicycle chain. Also, unlike chains that needs maintenance, a rubber belt is ready to ride and lasts many times longer than a bicycle chain. Not only is it maintenance free and lasts longer but it is arguably a smoother ride because a belt doesn’t have the tendency to skip or come off the cranks like a chain will. No dirty greasy chain and longer lasting means a superior value and a safer drive system that your child is less likely to get hurt with. I should also note that the photo of the bicycle in this ad does not show this but this bicycle DOES come with a belt guard (aka. chain guard) that can go over the belt drive to protect a little one from getting a shoe lace caught, etc... I didn't install mine but the fact that this comes with one is an outstanding, extra safety feature and affirms that this bicycle is really phenomenal for a first time rider.

Finally, the overall components on this bicycle ranging from the Tektro adjustable hand brakes to the Kenda tires are premium components. The bike’s light, aluminum frame, very smooth and quiet belt drive and aforementioned adjustable hand brakes are attributes associated with premium bikes that sell for $300-$400 and that makes this Belsize a tremendous value. In my view, this is clearly the best value kids bicycle available, bar none. I should also note that the bicycle comes with a manual for putting it together and it is quite easy to assemble as it really just requires putting the handlebar, front wheel, pedals and seat on. Not difficult at all. I should note that before purchasing, I had questions about the bicycle and A11N Sports Company who manufactures/sells the bicycle was extremely receptive and prompt in answering my questions. It gave me even further confidence in the quality of the product because the company selling the bike followed up, answered my questions and demonstrated excellent customer service. I can't say enough about this bicycle as my four year old is already up and riding on the same day it's received and he LOVES the bike!!

Review:
About a year ago I decided I wanted to ride to get back in shape. I live in an area that lends itself to bicycling, with lots of parks and destinations and bike paths, I felt a cruiser type bike was best. My wife purchased me a simple Kent that I really liked. Wanting her to join me, I went on a search for a bike for her to replace her single speed cruiser. I once owned a very nice aluminum Trek mountain bike I loved, and one of the things that attracted me initially to this bike was it also was aluminum. Once her 7 speed EVRYjourney (in blue) arrived, I was so impressed I bought one for myself.

I am 6'1 and my wife is 5'9. We bought a mens grey 7 speed, and a blue woman's 7 speed. I have put nearly 200 miles on mine, and my wife just over 100 so far. I waited to write this review until I was confident about how I felt about these bikes.

I really love this bike. I mean, I really love them both. The color is great, both of them are just stunning. I work from home and I have had two customers comment on the bikes when my garage was open. The laid back seat and frame design is very comfortable for the both of us. The rear rack is awesome, and I purchased the matching bags that sit atop the rack. Those bags are OK - they fit and look good, but would be nice if they were a little stiffer on the sides. I also purchased the handlebar bags, which hold a lock, and whatever else I need. They match well. I also really like the fact it has the screw mounts for a water bottle cage (Though I stuck a JBL flip in those, one matches the woman's blue teal color exactly). I also bought matching bells from sixthreezero, and those are awesome too. Plus a cupholder with a phone holder, because I want to "cruise" sometimes too. Not just work out. This review isn't about the accessories, but if it helps anyone, they match well and I would buy them again. I will say I love the rack and the ability to carry stuff to the park or to a friends house.

The seat, for me, is great. My wife feels hers is as good or better than any other bike she's had - but she is interested in one of the larger seats sixthreezero has that match the brown color she has now. We may try it for her. The grips on the handlebars feel great, and they look cool as well. The tires are a street type tire, and so far neither has gotten a flat. I had a number of flats on mine and my kids bikes in the past, and until I bought decent tires and tubes it seemed like it never stopped. Could just be good luck I guess.

Shifting, pedals, all that... Seems smooth. Im not so hardcore I would really have much opinion beyond the fact that I have had zero issues. I am very mechanically inclined, and I didn't have any trouble assembling these. I took my time and made sure everything was adjusted well, but in reality I didn't do much. The brakes and gearing was fine out of the box, I just fine tuned it.

This bike has brought a lot of joy into my life, and so far has enabled me to lose over 50 pounds. The level of comfort has drawn me to now ride it every day, for at least 6 miles. Now that I am used to riding, this bike makes me enjoy the ride and I forget I am working out. Item arrived in great shape with the bike and shipping box undamaged. Results will always vary depending on who handles one of these during shipment. Was purchased for a 10 year old boy who is 53-54" tall.

Upon final assembly, the brakes and rear derailleur needed to be tuned. No surprise there. Rims were mostly straight with only 10-15 mins of time spent truing them. Did spend longer than should have adjusting the handle bar. Most of the bike is of decent quality but felt the stem/bar assembly could be a better design for this price point. Besides the stem/bar assembly, the only issue I have with this bike is the fork. The fork is very stiff with limited travel and will be mostly useless for a 80-90 lb rider except for the most extreme trails. Perhaps it will "loosen" over time. He had a little trouble working through this bike's 21 speeds initially but is becoming easier to shift with each ride. This is his first trail-worthy bike and will be a nice transition into something bigger and better as he grows.

Has been in use for less than 2 weeks with no problems. Is a good value at the $168 price point especially if you can assemble and tune it yourself. Otherwise, consider taking this to a bike shop for assembly and setup. Properly tuned it will hold its own with bikes costing 3x more. Happy with the purchase but if more info had been available at the time, I would have purchased the Diamondback Octane 24 instead. At $245 currently, the Octane offers a lighter aluminum frame, more aggressive tires, replaceable hanger, and upgrades to the shifters, stem, seat and rear derailleur.

Purchased for $168 from Amazon in September 2015. Made in China.

I bought this directly from Sixthreezero in the 24” 3-speed model in to replace a 26” 3-speed bike that was just too big for me. The bike rides and shifts smoothly, and the coaster brake and handbrake work as expected. A nice advantage of the 3-speed is that it’s fairly low maintenance, since the gears are inside the rear hub. The riding position is upright and comfortable. Because of my need to have the seat so low, I don’t quite get full leg extension while pedaling, but I expected that. I’m still getting used to the overall feel of the bike, but the seat seems comfortable enough. This bike is a beach cruiser style with a rather heavy steel frame and wide tires, meant for relatively short, casual rides, best for paved roads and maybe some easy rail trails.

Review:
After reading many of the negative reviews on the Discover model, I wanted to weigh in as a long time owner. I have owned a Solitaire model since 2013, and have ridden it 2800+ miles. The Solitaire was WalMart's private labeled version of the Discover, with steel fenders, and trigger shifters, for which I paid $200. Comparable bike shop models were selling in the $4-500 range at the time. I rate it a solid 4 stars, and believe you would have to pay +$1K today for a 5* model.
My bike was assembled at the local store where I purchased it, so I expected having to tune it (wheel trueing, spoke tightening, brake, shifter, seat, and handlebar adjustments). Since it's initial tune I have had to adjust the derailers/shifters, and brakes as the cables stretched, and the pads wore (I have replaced the front and rear brake pads once). I have also replaced tires, and tubes, which brings me to the most common complaint of the negative reviews (tire/tube failures). I experienced two flat tires within the first 100 miles. What I discovered as the cause, were inconsistent spoke lengths, with a couple protruding through the spoke nuts, wearing through the rim band, and puncturing the inner tube. The recommended 60PSI tire pressures contributed to the failures. I doubt lower PSI ratings of balloon type tires would have resulted in failures (as quickly). The OEM tires and tubes are inexpensive, low quality (which is where most manufacturer cut costs). I have not experienced any peddle/crank issues, and have dis/reassembled them for routine bearing cleaning, and lubrication (as well as the axles and steering head). I always use threadlock compound on all fasteners. Other than typical wear item adjustments/replacements, routine maintenance, and cleaning, the bike has performed flawlessly.
This thing is built like a tank, and as others have stated is heavy in comparison to other hybrid/commuter models (which I attribute to its durability). It is also a tall bike (18" frame, with 700 series tires). I am 5'7" with a 31" inseam, and admittedly this bike is too tall for me. That said; it is comfortable, and enjoyable for me to ride. My riding style is recreational (exercise, exploring, and enjoyment), on secondary roads, and paved trails. My mid-season average speed is 10mph, which is plenty fast (at 63, and 190 lbs. I have no delusions of participating in the Tour`de Farce). As a "hybrid" it is a compromise between a commuter, and mountain bike. IMO it is a better commuter due to tire size, and hardtail frame (the spring in the seat post is no substitute for rear suspension for off road riding).
The only modifications I have made are upgrading to a more comfortable seat, and installation of mirrors, and lights. The only additional options on my wish list would be disc brakes, and a Bafang electric drive conversion, but I'll survive without them (I hope)!
I expect this bike will last me for the remainder of my riding years, and highly recommend it to others with similar expectations.

Review:
This review is in reference to the Pluto 2.0 version of this bike in 16 inch. The bike comes in a box partially assembled, and with some very basic knowledge it is possible to assemble it within 30 minutes - but I do not recommend you do this.

Even though this and other kids bikes from CHY-NAH are quite expensive, it has more to do with higher shipping costs than it does with quality. In fact, I'd say half of this bike's price is shipping. My point is that corners were cut, and thankfully, most of them were on assembly and not the bike's components themselves.

The frame is solid and looks good, decent tires, and the wheels are fine (not true, but who cares it's a kids' bike). Where the main problems lie, and this is likely the cause for many of the negative reviews, is that the bearings for both the crank and headset are poorly lubed and not properly adjust.

Headset
---------------------
This bike has a threaded fork (the part that holds the front wheel) with two bearings - one up top and one at the bottom of the steerer tube. On my bike, they were both poorly lubed and over-tightened. To fix this, you carefully remove the painted hex nut at the top of the steerer tube, and then under that is the actual headset which you should be able to unscrew with your hands. Once this is out you can remove the entire fork along with the bearings. I cleaned bearings and bearing cup surfaces with mineral spirits, then slathered on my favorite grease - lucas oil green (which seems to work great on everything even though it's marketed as being for heavy machinery). I then reassembled the front end.

When you tighten the fork nut (the nut that holds the fork; not the hex lock nut), it should tight enough so that there is no play or wobble in the fork, but no more. If if is over-tightened the bearings will bind and it will make a grinding sound. On this bike you can just hand-tight until it free of play, then back off slightly. When you put the lock nut back on (the hex one) you can tighten it with a wrench and this will cause that bit of slack to be taken up. Remember it should turn freely with little or no resistance. If you feel resistance, it's too tight. If it wobbles then it is too loose.

Crank
---------------------
Before removing the crank you will want to loosen the rear wheel, which means taking off one set of outer bolts and loosening the inner bolts plus the coaster-brake's anti-rotation screw on the left side. Do this and slide the wheel forward to slack the chain. You will also need to remove the plastic chain guard. I completely removed it because it is not necessary...and will only serve to frustrate future maintenance.

To remove the crank on this bike, you would remove the hex lock nut on the left side (opposite the side where the sprocket is), then, by using a flat head screwdriver and a hammer you tap to loosen and remove the crank bolt that holds the whole thing together. The crank bolt has two notches and you stick the screwdriver into one of the notches on an angle and tap the top of the screwdriver gently with a hammer to loosen this. It should not be tight. Once it's out, you can pull the entire crankset out through the right side.

Here, again, I cleaned the bearings and bearing surfaces with mineral spirits, lubed everything with my grease, and reassembled. Much as with the headset, when you go to tighten the crank bolt that holds it together it must no bind. You have to get it just right. Remember, if it spins freely without wobbling it's good. If it grinds or sticks when you fling it, you over-tightened. If it wobbles, it needs to be tightened more. This is really done by feel. Once the tension is good, tighten the hex locknut with a wrench to keep it in place.

Again, you may find that once the locknut is tightened your "just right" bearing tension is now binding. To fix this, loosen the locknut, back off slightly on the crankset bolt (there may be the slightest wobble) then re-tighten the locknut.

Front Brakes
---------------------------
The front brake pads were out of alignment with the rim, and they were maladjusted. The position of the brake handle was a bit far-off for tiny kid hands. I adjust the brake pads by slightly loosening the nut that holds them to the brake caliper then squeezing the caliper with my hands against the rim. Perfect alignment both times; the top of the brake pad should be as close to the top of the rim as it can be without rubbing on the tire. Do that and tighten.

Next, you will see a phillips screw sticking out side-ways on the brake handle. This lets you adjust the distance of the handle from the handle bar. By turning it clockwise it will lessen the gap, and that's probably what you want. I turned mine all the way in and it reduced the gap but in my view it's still a bit large for kids.

Lastly you can loosen the cable nut that holds the brake cable to the caliper, then squeeze the calipers together but not all the way, leaving about 1/2 inch gap between the rim and the pads. While holding this position, use your other hand to tug the brake cable and pull it tight, then tighten the bolt back up. Doing this will drastically reduce the free-play and the distance that the brake handle needs to be pulled to actually brake.

Chain Tension
---------------------
If you did all of the above, you will have loosened the chain. The proper tension for the chain is to have a bit of slack, which will prevent binding and wear on the sprockets as well as reduce the chance that it pops off. There's no rule for how this is done but slide the rear wheel back until the chain is taught, then nudge the wheel forward slightly until there is the slightest sag in the chain. The sag should barely be noticeable.

Everything Else
---------------------
The rest of the bike setup is your call. The handlebars can be angled and height-adjusted to fit the rider and the seat has a quick-adjust clamp. The height of the seat top should be even with the hip of the rider standing next to the bike, and you can make small adjustments from there.

Conclusion
---------------------
My overall opinion on this bike as far as children's bikes go is that it's very good for starting out, but most people are not bike builders like myself and thus are not going to do this extra work. Unfortunately for these kinds, this bike will probably not last much more than a few months if it is ridden often. The simple fact is that they will experience premature wear from under-lubed and over-tightened bearings in the crank and handlebars.
